text: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household:
Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah;
Issachar, Zebulun and Benjamin;
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All those who came from Jacob's own body numbered seventy persons, and Joseph was already in Egypt.

versions.text: All those descended from Jacob numbered seventy in all, and Joseph was already in Egypt.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew idiom "יֹצְאֵי יֶרֶךְ־יַעֲקֹב" (those who came out of Jacob's thigh/loins) is more specific than "descended from Jacob," and "numbered seventy in all" is redundant with "All."

text: Then Joseph died, and all his brothers, and that whole generation.
But the Israelites were fruitful and swarmed; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, and the land was filled with them.

versions.text: But the Israelites were fruitful and multiplied greatly; they increased and grew so strong that the land was filled with them.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has four verbs in a piling-up sequence (fruitful, swarmed, multiplied, grew strong) with "exceedingly, exceedingly" attached to the last. The current rendering drops the swarming imagery and turns the filling of the land into a result clause ("so strong that") rather than the independent statement it is in Hebrew.

text: Then a new king arose over Egypt, one who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, "Look, the people of Israel have become more numerous and stronger than we are.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will keep multiplying, and if war breaks out they will join our enemies, fight against us, and go up out of the land.

versions.text: Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will keep multiplying, and if war breaks out they will join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country."
versions.explanation: "Leave the country" is flat and loses the Hebrew verb עָלָה (go up), which carries exodus overtones central to the book. Rendering it "go up out of the land" preserves the wordplay foreshadowing the exodus.

text: So they set slave masters over them to crush them with heavy burdens, and they built the supply cities of Pithom and Rameses for Pharaoh.

versions.text: So they set taskmasters over them to oppress them with forced labor, and they built the supply cities of Pithom and Rameses for Pharaoh.
versions.explanation: שָׂרֵי מִסִּים are officers of forced labor/gangs, and בְּסִבְלֹתָם means "with their burdens" — the current wording collapses two distinct terms and loses the imagery of burdens which recurs later in the book (e.g., 2:11; 5:4).

text: But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread, until the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.
So the Egyptians made the Israelites serve as slaves with ruthless force,

versions.text: So the Egyptians drove the Israelites ruthlessly to work,
versions.explanation: "Drove the Israelites ruthlessly to work" splits the verb awkwardly for oral reading; the Hebrew hiphil means "made them serve/work." A smoother rendering also avoids the repetition with verse 14's ending.

text: and made their lives bitter with hard labor in mortar and brick and with all kinds of work in the fields. In every task they ruthlessly drove them.
Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one named Shiphrah and the other Puah,
"When you help the Hebrew women give birth and see them on the birthstool, if it is a boy, kill him; if it is a girl, let her live."

versions.text: "When you help the Hebrew women give birth and watch them on the birthstool, if it is a boy, kill him; if it is a girl, let her live."
versions.explanation: "Watch them" suggests mere observation; the Hebrew רָאָה here means to look/see (i.e., check the sex of the child). "See them" is more accurate and reads better.

text: But the midwives feared God, and they did not do as the king of Egypt had ordered them; they let the boys live.
So the king of Egypt summoned the midwives and asked them, "Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?"
The midwives answered Pharaoh, "Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women. They are vigorous, and they give birth before the midwife reaches them."

versions.text: The midwives answered Pharaoh, "Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women. They are strong, and they give birth before the midwife arrives."
versions.explanation: חָיוֹת conveys liveliness/vigor in childbearing rather than general strength (which would overlap with עָצוּם in vv. 7, 9, 20). Also "before the midwife reaches them" reflects אֲלֵהֶן ("to them").

text: So God dealt kindly with the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very strong.
And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families of their own.
Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every boy that is born you shall throw into the Nile, but every girl you shall let live."
